newsitem.title: USA: Potential jurors criticize media in bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Potential jurors criticize media in bombing case.

text.p: Potential jurors said on Friday they have either ignored or not noticed extensive publicity in the Oklahoma City bombing case -- undermining defence claims that the news media had harmed Timothy McVeigh's right to a fair trial.

As jury selection completed its first week, almost all of the first 30 potential jurors said they had an open mind about whether the 28-year-old defendant was guilty of planting the bomb that devastated the Alfred P. Murrah federal building and killed 168 people.

Most also said the media distorted the story, including an Hispanic woman health care company supervisor who said first reports about McVeigh's arrest made it look like white supremacist groups were behind the bombing.

But she said she was keeping an open mind because the "media often misquotes or misrepresents things." She said she thought the media took control of the O.J. Simpson murder trial "and the outcome was a result of the media."
A few potential jurors recalled seeing news reports about McVeigh allegedly admitting to his lawyers that he was responsible for the bombing but said they were able to put that out of their minds.

One man questioned on Friday said he gave that report short shrift, adding: "I'd probably put that in line with what I'd see in the (supermaraket tabloid) National Enquirer ... It didn't seem credible to me."

Defence lawyers, who have denied the confession reports, said their greatest fear was that pre-trial publicity would make it impossible for McVeigh to get a fair hearing. At one point, they wanted the trial moved to Alaska or Hawaii.

All jurors questioned so far vividly remembered April 19, 1995, -- the day a massive fuel and fertiliser bomb tore the glass face off the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people and injuring some 500 others. And many remember seeing McVeigh being paraded in an orange prison jumpsuit shortly after his arrest.

McVeigh was charged with the "use of a weapon of mass destruction" and the murder of eight federal officials. A second defendant, his former Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried separately later. Both pleaded not guilty.
Meanwhile, victims and relatives of those who perished in the bombing sought assurances from Judge Richard Matsch that he would not bar them from testifying even if they listen to the proceedings.

In a request filed with the federal court, the group urged Matsch to "make it clear" that he will not bar the victims from testifying during the penalty phase, when jurors will decide whether McVeigh should be executed or sentenced to life imprisonment.

Under congressional pressure, Matsch recently reversed himself and said the victims who planned to testify at the penalty phase could sit through the trial. But the victims feared that they might end up being excluded and sought a stronger clarification.
Generally people who testify at trials are not allowed to sit in the courtoom to prevent them being influenced by what they hear.

Several prospective jurors asked not to serve, offering up family commitments and opposition to the death penalty as reasons why they could not be on one of the most important trials in U.S. criminal history.
One potential juror and grandfather of 19 said he would not be able to pay strict attention to the evidence because he would be missing a long-awaited summer family reunion.
A woman whose husband's parents survived Nazi concentration camps in Europe, said she was incapable of voting for the death penalty if McVeigh was found guilty.
"I personally don't feel I'd be able to live with a decision of saying someone should die or live," she said.
